questions.prompt: For solar radiation at the peak of the solar spectrum (0.5 μm), at what approximate particle size is the scattering efficiency maximized? Assume a refractive index for water (1.33).
questions.answer: The scattering efficiency is maximized at approximately 0.3 μm for solar radiation at the peak of the solar spectrum (0.5 μm) with a refractive index of 1.33. Depending on the refractive index, the scatterng efficiency has a clear peak for particle radii approximately equal to the wavelength. This is Mie scattering See Fig. 11.1.

questions.prompt: An aerosol layer with single-scatter albedo of 0.8 above a black surface (albedo of zero) causes a negative radiative effect at the top of the atmosphere (TOA) of -2 W m\(^{-2}\). The cloud fraction is 0.7. What surface albedo would cause this aerosol layer to have a positive radiative forcing?
questions.answerInfo: This is an approximate answer based on the data in the figure. The figure shows that for a single-scatter albedo of 0.8 and a cloud fraction of 0.7, the surface albedo needs to be greater than approximately 0.24 for the aerosol layer to have a positive radiative effect at the TOA. Any scattering aerosol above a black surface will always cause a negative radiative effect at the TOA (more radiation reflected than by the surface alone). But above cloud, the slightly absorbing aerosol can cause a positive radiative effects.

questions.prompt: A sulfate aerosol layer with single-scattering albedo of 1.0 above a soil surface (albedo of 0.25) causes a negative radiative effect at TOA of -2 W m\(^{-2}\). The cloud fraction is 0.7. What single-scattering albedo would cause this aerosol layer to have a positive radiative effect?
questions.answerInfo: This is an approximate answer based on the data in the figure. The figure shows that for a aerosol with a single-scatter albedo of 1.0 (purely scattering) and a cloud fraction of 0.7, the radiative effect at the TOA is about -2 W m\(^{-2}\). Decreasing the single-scatter albedo to 0.8 would cause the aerosol layer to have a positive radiative effect.

parts.prompt: A sulphate aerosol layer with a single-scatter albedo of 1.0 is measured to transmit 36.8% of the incident solar radiation with the sun directly overhead. What is the intensity of the scattered solar radiation relative to the transmitted solar radiation? Assume an upscatter fraction of 0.5.
parts.label: (a)
parts.answerInfo: The transmitted solar radiation is 36.8% of the incident solar radiation, so optical depth of the layer is \(\tau = -\ln(0.368)\). The scattered solar radiation below the layer is \((1-\exp(-\tau)) \times (1 - 0.5) = 0.632 \times 0.5 = 0.316\). This is 88% of the transmitted solar radiation.

parts.prompt: How would the intensity of the scattered solar radiation change for a very dense aerosol layer with an optical depth of 5?
parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: The transmitted solar radiation would be extremely small (\(\exp(-5)\)). However, the amount of solar radiation scattered downward would still be about 50%.
